body.text: Australia may be headed for recession, former Federal Reserve economist says
In short:
The speed at which Australia's unemployment rate is rising has prompted warnings of a possible recession.
Previously unpublished RBA research shows RBA economists experimenting with the "Sahm rule" recession indicator.
What's next?
RBA researchers say the Sahm rule can be a better indicator of recession than the traditional "technical recession".
Australia's unemployment rate has surged to its highest level in five years, raising concerns the Reserve Bank's battle against inflation could tip the economy into recession.
But some economists say a unique recession indicator that tracks the speed unemployment is rising could be triggered as early as December if unemployment maintains its current rate of increase.
The so-called Sahm rule, created by former US Federal Reserve economist Claudia Sahm, is an early warning indicator designed to detect recessions quickly using changes in unemployment.

It captures periods of recession-like pain for workers — where unemployment rises quickly within a short timeframe — that can occur when economic activity is weak but not quite weak enough to meet the more traditional definition of recession.
Reserve Bank economists agree it is a more useful definition of recession for policymakers because it provides an earlier warning that something has gone awry in an economy.
Australia's unemployment rate is rising quickly
Australia's jobless rate jumped to 4.9 per cent in October, to its highest level since 2021. It was higher than economists' expectations.
Almost 44,000 jobs were lost last month, leaving more than 750,000 Australians unemployed.
In an exclusive interview with the ABC, Dr Sahm explained why, in her view, the speed at which unemployment rose mattered more than the monthly unemployment rate when thinking about recessions.
"Changes in the unemployment rate, particularly over the past year, are really the warning sign, and we often see that once the unemployment rate starts rising," she said.
"And even [with] a fairly modest amount, it can start to snowball.
"We see countries go into recession when the unemployment rate is high or when it's relatively low as well."
When asked if Australia could cross her "recession" threshold within six to 12 months, Dr Sahm said it was possible.
"It is entirely possible that that is where this is headed,"
"The question is, can the central bank cool things off enough, get inflation under control, and not get out of hand in the labour market?"
She said if rising unemployment started gaining momentum, it could "feed on itself and unemployment can go up a lot more".
"So it is a risk. It's a real risk. Central banks have a long history of doing too much, and we end up in recession."
RBA considered applying Sahm rule to Australian economy
The Sahm rule works like this for Australia's economy:

Take the average unemployment rate for the past three months of unemployment data, and if that number happens to be 0.75 percentage points higher than the lowest unemployment rate recorded in the past 12 months, a recession will likely begin.
Using that calculation, Australia's reading is now 0.6 percentage points, so it has not yet triggered the 0.75 percentage points threshold.

The ABC has also obtained a previously unpublished Reserve Bank research note from January 2020 that shows that RBA researchers had been considering how to apply the Sahm rule to Australia's labour market in the months before COVID-19 hit Australia six years ago.
In the United States, the Sahm rule threshold is 0.5 percentage points.
But when RBA researchers began experimenting with applying the Sahm rule to Australian data, they concluded a threshold of 0.75 percentage points would be more appropriate for Australia's economy.

They said the rule easily detected the more traditional "technical recessions" in Australia in the early 1980s and 1990s, but it would also classify the dotcom bust of 2001 and the global financial crisis as "mild" recessions.
They said that matched the reality that unemployment rose quickly enough in those periods to cause recession-like pain for Australian workers.
The graph below shows what the RBA researchers meant:
The 0.75 threshold is represented by the horizontal dotted line. The grey columns are technical recessions.
Every time the unemployment rate jumps above the horizontal dotted line, it is a Sahm recession.
RBA researchers also discussed the Sahm rule in this formal paper from 2024.
Is Australia already in recession?
Australia has traditionally defined a "technical recession" as six months in a row of contracting economic output.
However, when working with that definition, policymakers cannot confirm if an economy is in a technical recession for up to nine months after the recession has started.
Some economists argue that that definition of a "technical recession" can also fail to reflect the damage that can occur from economic weakness or abrupt but short downturns.
Independent economist Saul Eslake points to 1974, when Australia's economy contracted by 2 per cent in a single quarter but did not meet the two-quarter test.
Mr Eslake told the ABC that the Sahm rule provided a good early warning of a possible recession, preventing the need to wait for GDP figures to confirm a downturn months after the fact.
He said relying on GDP figures to identify a downturn meant "you're really looking in the rear-vision mirror rather than in the windscreen in order to see what's going on".
Even RBA governor Michele Bullock has acknowledged that people may soon feel they are living through a recession without one being recorded in the GDP figures.
Earlier this month, after lifting interest rates for the fifth time this year, she said the economy would probably slow down "markedly" in the coming months.
"It is going to make people feel like it's a recession because they feel poorer," she said.
Could RBA push Australia into recession?
With last week's data showing that Australia's unemployment rate jumped to 4.9 per cent in October, unemployment is steadily climbing towards the 0.75 percentage point threshold.

Mr Eslake said if the unemployment rate continued to drift upwards at the same rate as it had, on average, over the past six months (by 0.06 of a percentage point per month), then the Australian version of the Sahm rule would be triggered in December.
He said if that was to happen, it would be confirmed when the unemployment data was published on January 21.
Mr Eslake said he was not forecasting that the Sahm rule would be triggered in December, but it was a potential risk.
"If it were to come to pass, it would certainly change the economic debate in Australia, and prompt questions as to whether the RBA might have overdone the tightening of monetary policy," he wrote.
He sees excessive interest rate increases as one potential cause of an avoidable downturn.
The RBA has said it is not forecasting a recession at this stage.
In October, RBA chief economist Sarah Hunter told a parliamentary hearing that Australia's economic indicators did not suggest a recession was approaching in the near term.
